title: Given a Set of Requirements, Provision the Appropriate Cloud Resources

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Provisioning means selecting and creating the cloud resources needed by a workload.
There is not always one best cloud resource. The correct resource depends on the requirements.
CompTIA gives you eight major requirement categories: storage, performance, security, cost, availability, compliance, network, and compute.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Which requirement is driving the resource decision?
sections.callout: Find the strongest requirement first → provision resources that satisfy it without unnecessarily violating the others.

sections.title: Storage Requirements
paragraphs: Storage requirements determine how much data must be stored, how it needs to be accessed, how quickly it must respond, and how long it must be retained.
Different workloads may need high-performance storage, shared files, object storage, or large inexpensive capacity.
Think: How much data, what kind, and how fast?
sections.callout: If the scenario focuses on data capacity or access method → prioritize storage requirements.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
paragraphs: Performance requirements define how quickly or efficiently the workload must operate.
They can involve processing capability, storage speed, network performance, or response time.
A resource that is inexpensive but cannot meet application demand is not properly provisioned.
Think: How fast does this need to run?
sections.callout: If users or applications require specific speed or responsiveness → prioritize performance.

sections.title: Security Requirements
paragraphs: Security requirements determine which protections must exist around cloud resources.
They can affect decisions about network access, resource isolation, data protection, and system configuration.
Think: What must be protected, and from whom?
sections.callout: If protection or restricted access is the primary concern → prioritize security requirements.

sections.title: Cost Requirements
paragraphs: Cloud resources should provide the required capability without unnecessary spending.
Provisioning far more resources than necessary creates waste. Provisioning too little can create performance or availability problems.
Think: Meet the requirement without buying far more than the workload needs.
sections.callout: If the workload must stay within a specific budget → prioritize cost requirements while still meeting technical needs.

sections.title: Availability Requirements
paragraphs: Availability requirements determine how resilient a workload must be.
A business-critical application may require resources distributed so the service can continue when individual components fail.
Think: How bad would it be if this disappeared?
sections.callout: If the workload cannot tolerate significant downtime → prioritize availability requirements.

sections.title: Compliance Requirements
paragraphs: Compliance requirements can restrict where data resides, how it is protected, who can access it, and which controls are required.
A technically excellent solution is still wrong if it violates required compliance controls.
Think: Allowed by technology does not always mean allowed by policy or regulation.
sections.callout: If required standards or controls dictate the design → prioritize compliance.

sections.title: Network Requirements
paragraphs: Network requirements determine how systems and users communicate with the resource.
Considerations can include connectivity, bandwidth, latency, routing, and network isolation.
Think: Who needs to talk to whom, and how well must the connection perform?
sections.callout: If connectivity between resources is the main issue → prioritize network requirements.

sections.title: Compute Requirements
paragraphs: Compute requirements determine how much processing capacity the workload needs.
This can include CPU, memory, workload type, and the amount of processing.
Think: How much processing muscle does the application need?
sections.callout: If the application is CPU- or memory-constrained → prioritize compute resources.

sections.title: Requirements Work Together
paragraphs: A real scenario may contain several requirements at once.
For example, a customer-facing application may need to remain available, protect sensitive data, stay within a strict budget, and handle high traffic.
You cannot choose the solution based only on cost. You have to balance availability, security, performance, and cost.
The CompTIA-style skill is identifying which requirement eliminates the wrong answers.

rows: What data capacity, type, or access is needed?
How fast must the workload operate?
What controls or rules must be followed?
How much processing power is needed?

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Running out of disk capacity → Storage
Application response is too slow → Performance
Unauthorized access must be prevented → Security
CPU or memory is insufficient → Compute

entries.title: Performance vs. Compute
paragraphs: Compute can affect performance, but performance problems are not automatically compute problems.
A slow application could be limited by CPU, storage, or network. Identify the actual bottleneck before increasing compute.

entries.title: Security vs. Compliance
paragraphs: Security protects systems and data. Compliance satisfies required rules and controls.
A compliance requirement may require security controls, but the reason the control exists in the scenario matters.

entries.title: Availability vs. Performance
paragraphs: Availability asks whether the service is accessible. Performance asks how well it operates while accessible.
A slow service may still be available. A fast server that is offline is not available.

entries.title: Cost vs. Everything Else
paragraphs: The cheapest solution is not automatically correct. Choose the least costly solution that still meets all stated requirements.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Need more or faster data capacity → Storage requirement
Need faster workload response → Performance requirement
Need protection, isolation, or access control → Security requirement
Need to reduce spending → Cost requirement
Must survive failure or downtime → Availability requirement
Must satisfy a required standard or regulation → Compliance requirement
Need connectivity, bandwidth, or routing → Network requirement
Need more CPU or memory → Compute requirement
